title: AI selloff deepens as Asia's chip stocks post historic weekly losses
dek: US stock futures are lower again after Thursday's 2% drop in all three major indexes, with the Nasdaq leading declines as chipmakers and newly listed Anthropic slide before the open. Investors are also weighing a Fed widely expected to raise rates in December.
quick: Nasdaq 100 futures were down about 1.6% around 7 a.m. ET, S&P 500 futures about 0.7%, Dow futures roughly flat, after a sixth straight S&P 500 loss on Thursday.
Anthropic, which closed its record IPO day 17% above its $83 offer price, was down roughly 6% to 8% in premarket trading.
Asia had its worst week in years: Taiwan's market fell 6.2% Friday, capping its worst week since 1991; the Nikkei dropped about 5% and SoftBank about 14%.
AMD fell again before the bell after a short seller's report on its China links; Nvidia remains under pressure after California subpoenaed the company.
Rate futures price a December Fed hike as nearly certain; Fed Governor Waller speaks this morning and Governor Cook at midday.
Gold is at its lowest since September 2025 as real yields and the dollar climb; oil is slightly higher after Houthi strikes on Riyadh.

blocks.head: The AI trade keeps unwinding, and Anthropic's debut didn't stop it
blocks.what: Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT after raising about $81 billion, the largest IPO on record. Shares opened at $111.50 against an $83 offer price, peaked near $115 and closed at $97.17, up about 17%. The broader market went the other way: the S&P 500 fell 2.02% to 7,175.83 for a sixth straight loss, the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.25% and the Dow lost 1,101 points (2.19%) to 49,097, its first close below 50,000 since June. Before Friday's open, Anthropic was down roughly 6% to 8%, according to CNBC and Benzinga.
blocks.why: Megacap tech and chip stocks carry the most weight in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, so continued selling there drags the indexes even when the rest of the market holds up. Reports also cited news that Apple is building its own AI agent, a potential competitor for Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta.
blocks.watch: Whether dip buyers show up in Anthropic and the megacaps after the open, or whether Thursday's pattern of late-day selling repeats.

blocks.head: Chipmakers under pressure on several fronts: Nvidia, AMD and export rules
blocks.what: California Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia, examining whether its advanced chips or confidential information reached China and whether the company misled investors about that risk. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO last week after admitting to an affair; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO. CNBC reports Nvidia shares are down about 22% over the nine trading days since Huang's admission. Separately, AMD fell 7.7% Thursday and was down another 5% to 7% premarket after Hunterbrook Media, which disclosed a short position, alleged AMD firmware turned up at companies linked to a US-blacklisted firm; AMD disputes the allegations and says it follows export rules.
blocks.why: Semiconductors have led the market for years, and a combination of legal risk, short-seller scrutiny and tighter export controls is pushing investors to reprice them. The Commerce Department this week required licenses to ship advanced AI chips to data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, which could cut into chip sales to Asia.
blocks.watch: Any response from Nvidia to the subpoena, and whether chip losses spread further to equipment makers and AI-linked utilities and industrials.

blocks.head: Fed hike in December is now the base case
blocks.what: After a hotter-than-expected October consumer price report, fed funds futures put roughly 90% to 95% odds on a quarter-point rate increase at the December 8-9 meeting, with the rest on a half-point move, per CME FedWatch data cited by CNBC and others. The current target range is 3.75% to 4.00%. Governor Christopher Waller has said a half-point hike is likely necessary; New York Fed President John Williams has said conditions don't call for dramatic action. Minutes from the October meeting showed officials comfortable with raising rates in December.
blocks.why: Higher expected policy rates lift bond yields and the dollar, which weighs on richly valued growth stocks and on assets that pay no interest, such as gold and Bitcoin.
blocks.watch: Waller's remarks at 8:25 a.m. ET and Cook's at 12:15 p.m. ET for any hint about the size of December's move.

blocks.head: Thursday's data showed slowing factory activity and rising prices
blocks.what: The Philadelphia Fed manufacturing index fell to 6.3 from 20.9, a six-month low, while its prices-paid gauge jumped to 58.2 from 43.2, the highest since April. Initial jobless claims came in at 203,000, slightly above forecasts near 198,000, and continuing claims rose by about 70,000 to roughly 1.76 million.
blocks.why: Weaker activity combined with firmer prices is the mix that worries both stock and bond investors: it squeezes profit margins while keeping the Fed leaning toward tighter policy.
blocks.watch: Next week's October PCE inflation data and the second estimate of third-quarter GDP, both due Wednesday.

blocks.head: Retail earnings: solid numbers, cautious outlooks
blocks.what: Walmart beat estimates and raised its outlook Thursday, but the stock still slipped about 1%. Williams-Sonoma fell about 15% after its report. After the close, Ross Stores beat estimates but gave a holiday-quarter profit outlook below expectations, sending shares down about 5% late Thursday, and Intuit fell roughly 10% after hours on a second-quarter revenue forecast of $4.93 billion to $4.95 billion, below the roughly $5.11 billion analysts expected. Intuit also agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for about $3.68 billion.
blocks.why: Retailer guidance going into the holiday season is a read on consumer spending, which drives about two-thirds of US economic activity. Cautious forecasts add to pressure on consumer discretionary stocks, Thursday's weakest sector.

blocks.head: Middle East risk props up oil
blocks.what: Houthi forces struck targets in Riyadh, damaging the 80-story tower that houses Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund, according to the Wall Street Journal and Reuters-based reports. Iran's Revolutionary Guards navy said two tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude rose modestly Friday morning but was still headed for a third straight weekly loss as shipments through Hormuz have returned to roughly prewar levels.
blocks.why: Supply scares lift energy stocks and add to inflation worries, which feeds back into Fed expectations. So far, ample supply has kept oil's gains small.

blocks.text: Asia

Asian markets took the heaviest losses. Taiwan's Taiex fell about 6.2% Friday, ending its worst week since 1991 with a weekly drop of roughly 17%, according to reports citing Bloomberg. Japan's Nikkei 225 closed down about 5%, its lowest close since April, as SoftBank sank about 14% on its heavy exposure to AI investments. South Korea's Kospi fell 5.2% and slipped below 5,000. MSCI's index of Asia-Pacific stocks outside Japan was down about 8% for the week, on track for its steepest weekly fall since March 2020. Hong Kong and Shanghai also fell, though less sharply.

In Japan, core consumer inflation rose to its highest level this year as energy subsidies expired, CNBC reported, though it came in below the 2.3% Reuters-polled economists expected. Traders are increasingly betting on a Bank of Japan rate hike in December.
Europe

European stocks opened lower. Shortly after the open, Reuters data showed the Stoxx 600 down about 0.9%, Germany's DAX down about 1.3% and France's CAC 40 down about 0.9%, while London's FTSE 100 held up better with a 0.4% loss. European tech stocks fell about 2.7%, led by chip-equipment makers ASML, ASM International and BE Semiconductor. The region is heading for its worst week since March. The UK and EU hold a summit today, where the BBC reports a youth mobility deal and agreements on food trade and carbon emissions are expected.
Currencies

The dollar index was little changed near 103.8 in early trading, holding most of its recent strength as US rate-hike bets build. The yen firmed slightly to about 159 per dollar, just off the 160 level that traders watch for possible Japanese intervention, helped by bets on a BOJ hike. The euro was near $1.098 and the pound near $1.31, both slightly higher. China's yuan was steady around 6.67 per dollar.

Futures point to another lower open, with the selling again concentrated in technology. Around 7 a.m. ET, Nasdaq 100 futures were down about 1.6%, S&P 500 futures about 0.7% and Dow futures roughly flat, according to 24/7 Wall St.; earlier readings from Benzinga and TipRanks showed smaller declines, so the size of the gap has been widening through the morning. The tilt toward the Nasdaq reflects losses in chipmakers and AI names, while more defensive and value-heavy Dow components are holding steadier.

Volatility is elevated: the VIX closed Thursday at 28.44, up nearly 16% on the day. With the S&P 500 down six sessions in a row and Asia posting multi-year weekly losses, traders will watch whether the market finds support or whether Friday's options expiration adds to swings.

Treasury yields have eased this week as investors shifted money into bonds during the stock selloff, but they remain high. The 10-year yield was near 5.02% in early Asian trading and slipped just below 5% this morning, according to FXStreet, which put it down more than 13 basis points for the week. The 2-year was near 4.73% and the 30-year near 5.39% overnight. That leaves the 2-year to 10-year spread at roughly 28 basis points, a positive slope, meaning longer-term borrowing still costs more than short-term.

The Fed's message has shifted firmly toward tightening. Fed funds futures imply roughly a 90% to 95% chance of a quarter-point hike on December 9, with the remainder on a half-point move. Waller has argued the Fed may need to reverse last year's cuts and has said a half-point move is likely needed, while also floating a quarter-point hike paired with a clear signal of a January follow-up. Williams has pushed back on a larger move. Governor Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in October in favor of a hike. Waller has noted core inflation running at about a 3.5% annualized pace over the past three months, well above the Fed's 2% goal. Analysts note that two-year real (inflation-adjusted) yields have topped 2.4%, a sign of how restrictive conditions have become.

Thursday's sectors

All 11 S&P 500 sectors fell Thursday. Consumer discretionary was the worst, down about 3.0%, with weak retail reactions such as Williams-Sonoma adding to the pressure. Communication services fell about 2.9% as Alphabet and Meta dropped between 2% and 4%. Energy held up best, down about 0.7%, supported by firm oil prices. The breadth of the decline, with even defensive sectors lower, suggests broad selling rather than rotation from one group to another.
Pre-market movers

items: AMD: down about 5% to 7% after a second day of pressure from Hunterbrook's short report.
Taiwan Semiconductor (ADR): down about 4% after Taiwan's market plunge.
Anthropic: down roughly 6% to 8% a day after its IPO, as early buyers took profits.
Nvidia: lower again amid the California subpoena and the CEO transition.
Intuit: down about 10% on a revenue outlook below estimates; also selling Mailchimp.
Ross Stores: down about 5% on a soft holiday-quarter profit forecast.
Keysight: modestly higher after record quarterly revenue of $1.99 billion, up 41%, and guidance of $2.04 billion to $2.06 billion.
Gap: mixed after-hours reaction; earnings of $0.82 a share beat estimates of $0.78 with flat comparable sales.

blocks.text: Oil

Brent crude was near $92.60 and WTI near $83.70 early Friday, up a little over half a percent. The Houthi strikes on Riyadh and reported tanker mine strikes in the Strait of Hormuz are lifting prices, but WTI is still on course for a weekly drop of close to 6% and Brent about 3.5%, as Gulf exports have recovered and the stock selloff raises concerns about demand.
Gold

Gold has dropped sharply, trading near $3,515 to $3,530 an ounce, its lowest since September 2025 and on track for a weekly decline of roughly 9%, according to CoinDesk and other reports. Analysts point to climbing real yields and a firmer dollar as rate-hike odds rise; because gold pays no interest, higher real rates make it less attractive. Silver has fallen even harder over the past month.
Crypto

Bitcoin was trading in a choppy range just under $62,000, down about 1% overnight and roughly 28% lower for the quarter, according to CoinDesk. Ether was near $1,725, down about 2%. The same forces hitting gold and tech stocks, higher real yields and reduced appetite for risk, are weighing on crypto.

items: 10:00 a.m. ET — University of Michigan consumer sentiment, final November: forecast 51.7. The preliminary reading rose to 51.0 from 48.0, a three-month high.
10:00 a.m. ET — Michigan year-ahead inflation expectations, final: the preliminary reading eased to 4.3% from 4.7%. Any move back up would reinforce Fed hike bets.
Fed speakers: Waller (8:25 a.m.) and Cook (12:15 p.m.) are the main events for rates.
Monthly options expiration today could add to intraday swings.

blocks.text: Friday is a light day for earnings, with no S&P 500 heavyweights reporting. Thursday night's reports from Intuit, Ross, Keysight and Gap will drive more of today's moves.

blocks.text: Today closes out the week, so the focus shifts to next week, a short week for Thanksgiving. Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Zoom report Monday after the close, followed by November consumer confidence on Tuesday and Dell and HP after Tuesday's close. Wednesday is the heaviest day: October PCE inflation (the Fed's preferred gauge), the second estimate of third-quarter GDP, durable goods orders, new home sales and the Fed's Beige Book, plus Deere earnings in the morning. Markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early, at 1 p.m. ET, on Friday. With the Fed's December 8-9 meeting approaching, Wednesday's PCE report is likely the week's biggest test of rate-hike expectations.

bottom_line: Markets open Friday under pressure, with the AI and chip selloff spreading from Asia to Europe and US futures, while bond and rate markets price a December Fed hike. Waller's comments and Michigan inflation expectations are the main scheduled catalysts today.
